turns.question: When you wrote about the violet flowers, was that bit for Theo or for Jo?
turns.control_query: Who is addressed in the particular passage of Vincent’s letter that calls the irises violet?
turns.review: Distinguish the part addressed to Theo from the letter’s two addressees. Keep the same distinction in memory.

turns.question: Did the other subject you mentioned come from there too?
turns.control_query: Did the other subject in Vincent’s letter about the violet irises also come from the garden?
turns.review: Identify the lilac bush as another garden subject. Avoid placing it in this painting. A cached passage suffices.

turns.question: Which ingredient did the conservator say had faded in these petals?
turns.control_query: Which pigment did Getty’s conservator find had faded in Irises?
turns.review: Identify geranium lake as the faded red pigment. Attribute the finding aloud to the modern conservator and preserve the attribution in memory.

turns.question: So can you say that every trace of it is gone?
turns.control_query: Does conservation evidence establish that all the red pigment disappeared from every iris?
turns.review: The transcript says considerable fading. It does not establish that every trace vanished or that a specific amount remains. Address the follow-up personally and keep its limit in memory.

turns.question: You sent this off with some other work. What did you call that group in your letter?
turns.control_query: How did Vincent describe the group that included Irises in the letter enclosing the work?
turns.review: The artist called the group studies after nature. The number counts a group of studies, not versions of Irises.

turns.question: Was the letter definitely written on July 14?
turns.control_query: How exactly do the editors date Vincent’s July letter enclosing Irises with other studies?
turns.review: Give 14 or 15 July 1889, and attribute this dating to the edition rather than personal memory. Do not confirm one particular day. Preserve the uncertainty in memory.

turns.question: For me that pale bloom almost interrupts the rhythm of the picture.
turns.review: Receive the visitor’s reading as theirs. Avoid inventing the artist’s intentions or a personal historical recollection.

turns.question: Does my reaction tell us you planned it that way?
turns.control_query: Does historical evidence establish that Van Gogh intended the single pale iris to interrupt the painting’s rhythm?
turns.review: Keep the impression with the visitor and the historical intention open. A guide note may be relevant but cannot prove a motive.

turns.question: The flowers seem to spill out of the frame. What kind of prints has Getty connected that with?
turns.control_query: What print tradition does Getty relate to the cropped composition of Irises?
turns.review: Identify Japanese woodblock prints as a probable influence in Getty’s account. Do not claim certainty or a specific print.

turns.question: How sure are they about that link?
turns.control_query: How certain is Getty’s account of the influence of Japanese woodblock patterns on Irises?
turns.review: Resolve they to Getty and link to Japanese woodblock prints. Preserve probable rather than certain influence in speech and memory. A valid cached source can suffice.

turns.question: Could you give me something to try with the leaves rather than just staring at the petals?
turns.control_query: What looking exercise uses the path of a leaf and a petal in Irises?
turns.review: Offer the leaf-tracing comparison with a petal as a present-day looking invitation. Avoid attributing an exercise to Vincent’s historical intention.

turns.question: Thanks, I could follow the leaf much more easily that time.
turns.review: Respond naturally to the visitor’s feedback. Remember that the visitor found it easier; do not add a historical claim.

turns.question: Can you give me tomorrow’s first bus departure time from the Getty?
turns.control_query: What is the time of tomorrow’s first bus departure from the Getty?
turns.review: Avoid inventing a timetable or citing art evidence. A brief redirection is appropriate.
